gotcha_text: Landlords leverage vague relocation language to move medical practices into inferior suites that lack necessary medical infrastructure or patient accessibility. This maneuver allows them to reposition high-value anchor tenants while forcing your practice into suboptimal, low-visibility locations.
fix_text: Tenant Pulse identifies ambiguous 'comparable' definitions and provides precise language to mandate specific utility and accessibility standards. Our tool ensures your lease prohibits any move that compromises clinical functionality or patient convenience.
deep_dive_html:
For medical practitioners, a lease is far more than a mere real estate agreement; it is a critical component of your clinical operational blueprint. Relocation clauses, often buried within the 'Miscellaneous' or 'Use' provisions, grant landlords the unilateral right to move your practice to another unit within the development. The primary danger lies in the ambiguity of the term 'comparable space.' Without rigorous, technical definitions, a landlord can legally move a specialized surgical suite into a space that lacks the necessary plumbing, electrical load, or ADA-compliant ingress, effectively destroying your practice's clinical utility and patient safety standards.

Beyond physical infrastructure, relocation can catastrophically disrupt the 'patient flow' essential to your revenue stream. A move from a ground-floor corner suite with high visibility to a second-floor interior unit—even if the square footage is identical—represents a devastating loss of organic patient acquisition. Landlords frequently leverage these clauses to 'make room' for larger, higher-rent anchor tenants, treating your established medical practice as a movable piece on a chessboard to maximize their portfolio's rent roll.

Implementing Structural Protections

To neutralize this threat, your lease must move beyond vague 'comparability' and establish a strict, non-negotiable checklist of requirements for any proposed relocation. A successful defense requires that the landlord proves the new space meets the following criteria:

  • Mandating that 'comparable' includes identical visibility, signage rights, and floor-plate efficiency.
  • Requiring the landlord to bear 100% of all build-out, permitting, and specialized medical-grade moving costs.
  • Demanding full reimbursement for 'business interruption' and documented lost revenue during the transition period.
  • Ensuring the new space meets all specific medical-use zoning, specialized HVAC, and utility requirements.
  • Securing the right to terminate the lease if the new space fails to meet these technical standards.
